blocks.text: I. The first passage, as far as I recall, is Levit. XIV, 4., where the leper who has been cleansed is commanded to offer to God δύο ὀρνίθια ζῶντα καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia zōnta kathara], that is, as some would have it, two living clean little hens. Origen, Homily 8 on Leviticus: He commands that two living hens be taken for him who is cleansed. And a little later: These two hens also seem to me here to bear a certain likeness to the two [II, 677] goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent out into the wilderness: for so here too, of the two hens one is sacrificed and the other is released into the field. And again: He who is purged of leprosy and offers hens. Likewise: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding, through which the purification of the sinner is effected, of which it is written, “How often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen,” etc. Since these words are ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], they seem to need reading thus: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding of the hen, through which, etc. That is, by those hens he wants Christ to be signified, who in the Gospel compares himself to a hen. Hence the addition: The hen shall be killed in an earthen vessel into which running water has been put, so that water too may be taken for the purification, and the fullness of the mystery may be fulfilled in the water and the blood which is said to have come forth from the side of the Saviour. And much more about this same hen can be read in what follows. In the ninth volume of the Works of Jerome, the author of the thirty-ninth Epistle, On the various kinds of leprosies, following the same view, says: But why are two hens commanded to be offered for the cleansing of leprosies? The two hens seem to indicate the soul and the flesh: but one hen, he says, you shall kill, the other you shall wash and release, etc. Yet in the Hebrew text nothing is said of hens: God merely commands that in the purification of leprosy שתי צפורים be taken, two birds (or two little birds, or two sparrows), which the Greeks rendered not badly as δύο ὀρνίθια [dyo ornithia], but with an ambiguous word, which in the age of the Fathers meant only hens, or for the most part hens. Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 4, where he treats of the gallinaceous kind: Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ὄρνιθας, καὶ ὀρνίθια νῦν μόνον ἡ συνήθεια καλεῖ τὰς θηλείας· [alla mēn kai ornithas, kai ornithia nyn monon hē synētheia kalei tas thēleias] Now indeed the custom has prevailed that only the females of cocks (that is, hens) are called ὄρνιθες [ornithes] and ὀρνίθια [ornithia]. This gave occasion to the error. Yet Plutarch, nearly contemporary with Athenaeus, says in the Artaxerxes that the rhyndax is μικρὸν ἐν Πέρσαις ὀρνίθιον [mikron en Persais ornithion], that is, a small little bird among the Persians. And that in the Law δύο ὀρνίθια καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia kathara] are two clean little birds ought to have been clear enough even to those ignorant of the Hebrew language. For the lawgiver would not have said two clean hens. That epithet would have been pointless, since every hen is clean.
